<br>

### Rate 6's block structure is regressive

**Q.** Besides Rate 6's discount being too low, what problems does the rate's block structure create?

**A.** Targeting lower rates directly to incremental heat pump load is a laudable goal, and a block rate structure would appear to be a natural way to do it. But the design rests on an implicit assumption: that every customer's pre-heat-pump electricity use is approximately 700 kWh per month, so that kWh above the threshold can serve as a proxy for incremental heat pump load. If that assumption held, the design would work — the threshold would neatly separate base load from heat pump load for everyone.

But in reality, the Company's fossil-fuel-heated customers vary far too widely in their pre-heat-pump electricity use for a single cutoff to work. When a customer's base load deviates from the threshold, the discount is misallocated in one of two ways:

1. **Discount leakage**: when a customer's base load is *below* the threshold, some of their incremental heat pump electricity lands in Block 1 at the full rate, and they receive less discount than intended.
2. **Windfall discount**: when a customer's base load is *above* the threshold, some of their pre-existing consumption — unrelated to the heat pump — gets the Block 2 discount as an unintended windfall.

These **misallocations** are not specific to the 700 kWh threshold — they are inherent to any block design with a fixed cutoff applied to a heterogeneous population.

And as I will show, these misallocations produce two concrete **harms**: 1. the block design is regressive, because lower-income customers have lower base loads; and 2. it is systematically biased against natural-gas customers, who also have lower base loads. (The seasonal rate I propose in Section X avoids these two harms entirely, and ultimately does a better job of delivering a discount that is proportional to each customer's incremental heat pump load.)

I will address each of these harms in turn, after providing examples of the misallocations.

<br>

**Q.** Can you provide examples to illustrate discount leakage and windfall discount, the two types of discount misallocations introduced above?

**A.** Consider two delivered-fuel homes, both of which switch to a heat pump and add the same 500 kWh per month of incremental winter electricity.

**Discount leakage.** Home A uses 400 kWh per month before the heat pump — well below the threshold. After the retrofit, it uses 900 kWh. Under Rate 6, the first 700 kWh is billed at the Block 1 rate (`{python} f"{th.block1_rate_cents:.1f}"` ¢/kWh) and only the last 200 kWh gets the Block 2 rate (`{python} f"{th.block2_rate_cents:.1f}"` ¢/kWh). Of the home's 500 kWh of heat pump load, only 200 kWh — 40% — lands in Block 2. The other 300 kWh is billed at the full Block 1 rate. The discount *leaks* — it fails to reach most of the incremental heat pump load it was designed for.

**Windfall discount.** Home B uses 900 kWh before the heat pump — well above the threshold. After the retrofit, it uses 1,400 kWh. Under Rate 6, the first 700 kWh is again Block 1, and the remaining 700 kWh gets Block 2. All 500 kWh of heat pump load lands in Block 2, but Home B also gets the Block 2 discount on 200 kWh of its pre-existing base load. That is a *windfall* — a discount on electricity that has nothing to do with the heat pump.

The threshold treats both homes the same, but the economic outcomes are very different: Home A receives `{python} f"{th.block_discount_cents:.1f}"` ¢/kWh of discount on only 40% of its heat pump load, while Home B receives that discount on 100% of its heat pump load *plus* an additional windfall on existing consumption.

<br>

**Q.** How well does the 700 kWh assumption hold for delivered-fuel customers?

**A.** Poorly. I examined the distribution of average monthly pre-heat-pump electricity use during winter across the full ResStock sample of delivered-fuel-heated customers. @fig-ribbon-df-base-only ranks every delivered-fuel customer from lowest to highest base load, and plots this base load against Rate 6's 700 kWh threshold.

:::{.column-page-inset-right}
{{< embed notebooks/rate6_threshold.qmd#fig-ribbon-df-base-only >}}
:::

The _average_ monthly winter base load for these customers is `{python} f"{th.winter_kwh_mean_delivered:,.0f}"` kWh per month, which matches the 700 kWh threshold well.

For the threshold to work well, however, most customers' base load would need to cluster near 700 kWh. They do not. (The lines in the chart would need to be largely parallel.) Only `{python} pct(th.pct_within_100_of_threshold_df)` of delivered-fuel homes have a base load between 600 and 800 kWh. (The gray line in @fig-ribbon-df-base-only.) The middle 80% of homes range from `{python} f"{th.winter_kwh_p10_delivered_bldg:,.0f}"` to `{python} f"{th.winter_kwh_p90_delivered_bldg:,.0f}"` kWh — a sixfold spread. With so much variation in customer base load, no single threshold can accurately separate base load from heat pump load for most people.

<br>

**Q.** Given this wide variation in base load among delivered-fuel-heated customers, how much discount leakage and windfall actually occurs under the 700 kWh threshold?

**A.** @fig-ribbon-df-full adds post-heat-pump consumption to the previous chart. The chart visualizes which homes experience discount misallocations: blue is incremental load correctly in Block 2, orange is incremental load trapped in Block 1 (discount leakage), and yellow is base load spilling into Block 2 (windfall).

:::{.column-page-inset-right}
{{< embed notebooks/rate6_threshold.qmd#fig-ribbon-df-full >}}
:::

Both misallocation problems are prevalent.

**Discount leakage** (orange) affects `{python} pct(th.pct_any_orange_df)` of delivered-fuel homes — their base load is below 700 kWh, so some of their incremental heat pump load is trapped in Block 1 at the full rate. Among those homes, the median amount of leaked HP load is `{python} f"{th.median_trapped_kwh_df:,.0f}"` kWh per month.

**Windfall discount** (yellow) affects `{python} pct(th.pct_any_yellow_df)` — their base load is above 700 kWh, so some of their pre-existing consumption gets the Block 2 discount. Among those homes, the median windfall is `{python} f"{th.median_windfall_kwh_df:,.0f}"` kWh per month.

<br>

**Q.** Is discount misclassification correlated with income?

**A.** Yes. Among delivered-fuel homes, base load and income are positively correlated (weighted Pearson *r* = `{python} f"{th.income_base_load_corr_df:.2f}"`). Higher-income homes tend to be larger, have more appliances, and generally consume more electricity before installing a heat pump. And this has direct consequences for the discount misallocation.

@fig-ribbon-df-by-income shows the same chart for each income tercile of delivered-fuel homes.

:::{.column-page-inset-right}
{{< embed notebooks/rate6_threshold.qmd#fig-ribbon-df-by-income >}}
:::

Among low-income delivered-fuel homes, `{python} pct(th.pct_any_orange_df_low)` experience discount leakage — their base load is below 700 kWh, so much of their HP load is trapped in Block 1 at the full rate. Only `{python} pct(th.pct_any_yellow_df_low)` receive a windfall. Among high-income homes, the picture reverses: only `{python} pct(th.pct_any_orange_df_high)` experience discount leakage (and the leakage is smaller, as a share of their incremental load) while `{python} pct(th.pct_any_yellow_df_high)` receive a windfall on pre-existing base load.

Rate 6's Block 2 discount is designed to reduce every customer's incremental heat pump bill by **`{python} pct(th.block_discount_pct, 1)`**, because it lowers the price charged for each of those kWh by `{python} pct(th.block_discount_pct, 1)` — from `{python} f"{th.block1_rate_cents:.3f}"` ¢/kWh to `{python} f"{th.block2_rate_cents:.3f}"` ¢/kWh. Because of discount leakage, low-income delivered-fuel homes see their incremental HP bills reduced by only **`{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_df_low, 1)`** on average (even after including the `{python} pct(th.pct_any_yellow_df_low)` of low-income homes that receive a windfall.) High-income homes see a **`{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_df_high, 1)`** reduction in their incremental HP bills, on average — more than intended, because most get the full discount on their heat pump load, plus an additional windfall on pre-existing base load.

<br>

**Q.** Does Rate 6's block design have a regressive impact?

**A.** Yes. A rate design feature is regressive when it delivers a larger benefit to higher-income customers than to lower-income customers. In this case, the benefit is a **proportional bill discount**: Rate 6 aims to give all delivered-fuel customers a `{python} pct(th.block_discount_pct, 1)` on their heat pump bill, because it lowers the all-in Block 2 rate by `{python} pct(th.block_discount_pct, 1)`. But Rate 6 does not deliver proportional bill discounts to all customers. Instead, the percent reduction in incremental heat pump bills increases with income — `{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_df_low, 1)` for the lowest-income third of delivered-fuel homes, `{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_df_mid, 1)` for the middle third, and `{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_df_high, 1)` for the highest-income third — against a design target of `{python} pct(th.block_discount_pct, 1)` for all.

Ultimately, the reason Rate 6's block design is regressive is straightforward: higher-income homes have higher base loads, which places them above the 700 kWh threshold; lower-income homes have lower base loads, which keeps them below it. The threshold converts the correlation between income and base load into a correlation between income and savings.

<br>

**Q.** Could Rate 6's regressive impact be avoided by choosing a different threshold?

**A.** No. Regressivity is an inherent problem of _any_ block rate with a one-size-fits-all threshold, not just 700 kWh.

Moving the threshold lower would reduce leakage but increase windfall; moving it higher would do the reverse. In fact, 700 kWh is close to the threshold that minimizes total misallocation.[^threshold-optimum]

But even when misallocations are minimized, they are far from eliminated, because base loads vary so widely across homes. And the fact that this variation in base load is correlated with income ensures that lower-income people will tend to get discount leaks, and higher-income people will tend to get windfalls — even if the "best" threshold is chosen.

[^threshold-optimum]: This is because 700 kWh is near the mean base load of delivered-fuel homes, and at that point leakage and windfall are roughly equal.

<br>

**Q.** In Section VII, I showed that Rate 6's discount is far smaller than it could be. If the discount were set at the marginal cost floor (as in modified Rate 6), would the regressive impact of the block design go away — since all customers would be getting a much larger benefit?

**A.** No — it gets worse. As I showed above, the threshold systematically gives low-income homes only `{python} pct(th.total_benefit_ratio_df_low)` of their intended savings, while high-income homes get `{python} pct(th.total_benefit_ratio_df_high)`.[^intended-savings] These _percentages_ arise from the threshold, and do not change with the discount size. However, a bigger discount applied through the same percentages produces a bigger gap in what customers actually receive.[^lockstep]

[^intended-savings]: A customer's "intended savings" is what they would receive if the threshold perfectly separated their base load from their heat pump load — that is, if every kWh of incremental HP consumption landed in Block 2 and none of their base load did. The ratio shown (e.g. `{python} pct(th.total_benefit_ratio_df_low)` for low-income homes) is the each customers's actual savings divided by their intended savings, averaged across the customers in an income group. A home with mostly leakage might capture only 20%; a home with a large windfall might capture 150%. The group average tells you whether the threshold delivers the right amount of savings to that population on balance — and for low-income homes, even after including homes that receive windfalls, the answer is barely more than half.

[^lockstep]: The arithmetic: low-income homes capture `{python} pct(th.total_benefit_ratio_df_low)` of their intended savings, so their effective bill reduction is `{python} pct(th.total_benefit_ratio_df_low)` × `{python} pct(th.block_discount_mod_pct)` = `{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_mod_df_low)`. High-income homes capture `{python} pct(th.total_benefit_ratio_df_high)`, so theirs is `{python} pct(th.total_benefit_ratio_df_high)` × `{python} pct(th.block_discount_mod_pct)` = `{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_mod_df_high)`. The same ratios that produced an `{python} f"{(th.effective_bill_reduction_df_high - th.effective_bill_reduction_df_low)*100:.0f}"` percentage-point gap under a `{python} pct(th.block_discount_pct)` discount produce a `{python} f"{(th.effective_bill_reduction_mod_df_high - th.effective_bill_reduction_mod_df_low)*100:.0f}"` percentage-point gap under a `{python} pct(th.block_discount_mod_pct)` discount.

Under Rate 6 as proposed, the Block 2 discount is `{python} f"{th.block_discount_cents:.1f}"` ¢/kWh, or `{python} pct(th.block_discount_pct)` of the Block 1 rate. As I showed above, low-income homes see an effective bill reduction of only `{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_df_low)`, while high-income homes see `{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_df_high)` — a `{python} f"{(th.effective_bill_reduction_df_high - th.effective_bill_reduction_df_low)*100:.0f}"` percentage-point gap, driven entirely by the threshold's inability to consistently separate base load from heat pump load.

Under the modified Rate 6 I presented in Section VII — with Block 2 rates for upstream distribution, local distribution, and transmission all set at marginal cost — the discount grows to `{python} f"{th.block_discount_mod_cents:.1f}"` ¢/kWh, or `{python} pct(th.block_discount_mod_pct)` of the Block 1 rate. If the threshold worked perfectly, every customer's incremental heat pump bill would fall by `{python} pct(th.block_discount_mod_pct)`. But the same threshold imprecision applies: low-income homes would see only a `{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_mod_df_low)` reduction, while high-income homes would see `{python} pct(th.effective_bill_reduction_mod_df_high)` — a `{python} f"{(th.effective_bill_reduction_mod_df_high - th.effective_bill_reduction_mod_df_low)*100:.0f}"` percentage-point gap.[^lockstep]

In other words, fixing Problem 1 (the discount being too small) without fixing Problem 2 (the block structure misallocating the discount) actually makes the regressivity _five times worse_ in absolute terms.

<br>

### Rate 6's block structure disadvantages natural-gas customers

**Q.** If Rate 6 were applied to natural gas customers, how would its 700 kWh threshold impact them?

**A.** The 700 kWh threshold systematically disadvantages natural-gas-heated customers who install heat pumps. This is a distinct problem from regressivity: the threshold is set at a level that largely excludes natural-gas homes from the discount.

<br>

**Q.** Why does the threshold disadvantage natural-gas customers?

**A.** Because natural-gas-heated homes use much less electricity before installing a heat pump than delivered-fuel-heated homes. The average pre-HP winter base load for natural-gas homes is `{python} f"{th.winter_kwh_mean_natgas:,.0f}"` kWh per month — nearly `{python} f"{th.winter_kwh_mean_delivered - th.winter_kwh_mean_natgas:,.0f}"` kWh below the 700 kWh threshold. By contrast, delivered-fuel homes average `{python} f"{th.winter_kwh_mean_delivered:,.0f}"` kWh, close to the threshold itself.

This is likely by design, as the Company intends Rate 6 to only be available to delivered fuel customers. As explained in Section VI, their justification for not reducing the overpayments experienced by natural-gas-heated customers who install heat pumps — their total energy bills might go up — ignores the fact that the main reason bills go up _is_ that these customers are being overcharged.

I advocate for the Company's heat pump rate to be available to all customers installing heat pumps, including those who currently heat with natural gas. So let's examine how the current 700 kWh threshold would affect these customers, and whether it can be improved.

@fig-ribbon-fuel-comparison compares how Rate 6's 700 kWh threshold classifies load for the two fuel groups side by side.

:::{.column-page-inset-right}
{{< embed notebooks/rate6_threshold.qmd#fig-ribbon-fuel-comparison >}}
:::

The key question is: of a home's incremental heat pump load, what share actually lands in Block 2 and receives the discount? If the threshold worked perfectly, the answer would be 100% for every home — all incremental load would be blue. For the median delivered-fuel home, it is `{python} pct(th.median_capture_rate_df)`. In other words, the threshold largely works for over half of these customers. (It does not work for everyone: roughly a third of delivered-fuel homes lose a fifth or more of their intended discount, and as the income analysis above established, these are disproportionately lower-income homes.)

For the median natural-gas home, however, only `{python} pct(th.median_capture_rate_ng)` of incremental HP load receives the discount — the threshold fails. And `{python} pct(th.pct_capture_below_05_ng)` of natural-gas homes — nearly 1 in 4 — would receive essentially no discount at all, because their post-HP consumption never reaches 700 kWh. Among delivered-fuel homes, only `{python} pct(th.pct_capture_below_05_df)` fare that poorly.

<br>

**Q.** What does this mean in practice for a natural-gas customer who installs a heat pump under Rate 6?

**A.** Rate 6's Block 2 discount is designed to reduce every customer's incremental heat pump bill by `{python} pct(th.block_discount_pct, 1)`. For customers that used to heat with natural gas, the 700 kWh threshold traps so much heat pump load in Block 1, that these customers would see their incremental heat pump bill reduced by only **`{python} pct(th.median_effective_bill_reduction_ng, 1)`**, on average — roughly half of the intended discount. The typical delivered-fuel home, by contrast, would see a **`{python} pct(th.median_effective_bill_reduction_df, 1)`** reduction, on average, much closer to the intended `{python} pct(th.block_discount_pct, 1)` bill reduction.

This is the underlying reason why Rate 6 doesn't significantly move the needle for post-heat pump bill outcomes. Even with Block 2 rates set at the marginal cost floor, natural-gas customers receive roughly half the intended discount — and that is why more than half of them would still face higher total energy bills after switching to a heat pump.

<br>

**Q.** Could the Company lower the threshold so it works better for natural-gas customers?

**A.** Lowering the threshold helps natural-gas homes, but it sends windfall discount to delivered-fuel homes. @fig-ribbon-threshold-comparison illustrates the trade-off. The top row shows the current 700 kWh threshold; the bottom row lowers it to `{python} f"{th.threshold_ng_kwh:.0f}"` kWh — the natural-gas mean base load.

:::{.column-page-inset-right}
{{< embed notebooks/rate6_threshold.qmd#fig-ribbon-threshold-comparison >}}
:::

The bottom-right panel shows the improvement for natural-gas homes: much more blue, meaning their heat pump load now reaches Block 2. Their capture rate rises from `{python} pct(th.total_benefit_ratio_ng)` to `{python} pct(th.tbr_ng_at_ng_mean)`. But the bottom-left panel shows the cost: `{python} pct(th.pct_any_yellow_df_at_ng_mean)` of delivered-fuel homes now receive a windfall (yellow), and their capture rate balloons to `{python} pct(th.tbr_df_at_ng_mean)` — meaning the delivered-fuel population as a whole receives far more discount than intended, despite the fact that this population needs _less_ help than that switching from natural gas, from a bill savings standpoint.

<br>

**Q.** Are block rates with one-size-fits-all thresholds inherently biased against natural-gas-heated and lower-income customers switching to heat pumps?

**A.** Yes. For any given threshold that is chosen, block rates will deliver smaller-than-intended savings to the customer groups that need them most — lower income and natural-gas-heating customers — and larger-than-intended savings to the customer groups that need them least — higher income and delivered-fuel-heating customers.

This trade-off is inescapable: the only way to increase the savings received by lower income and natural-gas-heated customers is to lower the threshold, which in turn delivers even larger savings to higher income and delivered fuel customers.

<br>

**Q.** Is it possible to design a block rate that avoids these biases?

**A.** Yes, by moving to per-customer thresholds, rather than a single residential class-wide number. There are at least three ways to implement per-customer thresholds.

The most accurate would be **separately metering** the heat pump. In addition to the cost, this approach would add significant friction to customer enrollment, and rule out auto-enrollment entirely, of both existing and new heat pump customers. (As I will discuss in Section XII, auto-enrollment is essential to the success of the rate.)

Another option would be **circuit-level energy monitors** such as Sense or Emporia Vue (often called non-invasive submeters, in regulatory contexts). These would be lower cost, and may be compatible with auto-enrollment of new heat pump customers: contractors installing heat pumps under EnergizeCT already interact with each home, and opt-out energy monitor installation and Rate 6 enrollment could become part of the installation process. Auto-enrollment of the Company's _existing_ heat pump customers would remain impractical, however. And while these monitors could accurately measure incremental heat pump load, they likely would not integrate into the Company's billing software. Savings would need to be delivered as credits administered by a third party, rather than lower rates on the customer's bill.[^ev-managed-charging]

[^ev-managed-charging]: This is essentially the model that utilities already use for EV managed charging. Con Edison's SmartCharge New York program (administered by ev.energy) pays EV drivers via Venmo or PayPal for off-peak charging. WeaveGrid administers similar programs for BGE, Pepco, Delmarva, Potomac Edison, and Orange & Rockland, delivering incentives via Venmo, gift cards, or bill credits. In all cases, the third party manages the device telemetry and delivers savings outside the utility's billing system.

The cheapest and most frictionless option would be a **software-based solution**. The Company could estimate per-customer thresholds from their meter data: for instance, by averaging each calendar month's consumption over the past 3–5 years (the average of January 2024, January 2025, and January 2026 becomes the January threshold, and so on). The Company would then subtract the threshold from each month's post-installation consumption to estimate incremental heat pump load, apply the Block 2 rate to that load, and generate the bill. This could be done within the billing system itself — Rate 6 already uses a block threshold as a billing determinant, and making that determinant customer-specific rather than class-wide is standard functionality in utility billing platforms.[^billing-system] Alternatively, a third party could perform the baseline estimation and load separation, and deliver the resulting savings as a credit outside the bill.

[^billing-system]: Utility billing platforms such as SAP IS-U and Oracle CC&B already support customer-specific billing determinants — demand ratchets, for example, are set per meter. A per-customer block threshold would be implemented the same way: stored as a customer attribute and referenced by the rate calculation engine each billing cycle.

All three approaches add complexity — whether in hardware, software, or administration. The first two make auto-enrollment difficult to impossible, which would lead to single-digit rate enrollment and leave the cross-subsidy largely in place.

In short: in order to achieve a block rate with per-customer thresholds that heat pump customers could be auto-enrolled into, the Company would either need to commit to a software-based solution, or to EnergizeCT contractors installing circuit-level energy monitors whenever they install heat pumps.

However, a simpler alternative to per-customer thresholds exists that achieves largely the same result: a seasonal rate design that lowers volumetric charges for heat pump customers in winter, without relying on a block threshold at all. I present exactly such a rate in the next section.

## X. Proposed Rate Design: Rate HP

<br>

**Q.** What do you propose to address the overcharging of heat pump customers?

**A.** I recommend that the Company create a new rate schedule, Rate HP, for residential customers with heat pumps. Rather than using a block design, Rate HP would lower the volumetric rates for distribution and transmission during the winter months (November through March), when the incremental heat pump load occurs. Rate 1's summer rates, generation rates, and the fixed customer charge would be **unchanged**. All customers with heat pumps would be eligible to enroll in Rate HP, regardless of whatever heating system they had before.


**Q.** How is Rate HP intended to affect revenue collection from heat pump customers?

**A.** The purpose of lowering winter rates is to bring the incremental revenue the Company collects from customers installing heat pumps in line with the incremental marginal costs those heat pumps actually cause (while preserving the revenue previously collected from their base load). As I showed in Section III, heat pump customers are overcharged because volumetric rates charge far more per incremental kWh than the incremental marginal T&D cost those kWh cause. Rate HP corrects this by reducing volumetric delivery rates in winter, the season when incremental heat pump load is concentrated, in order to achieve bills consistent with cost-causation: that is, bills that get as close possible to each customer's pre-heat pump T&D bill, plus their incremental marginal T&D cost caused by the heat pump.


**Q.** What is the ultimate objective of Rate HP?

**A.** By removing the overcharge for heat pump customers (on average), the ultimate objective of Rate HP is to fix  the intra-class equity and building electrification policy problems that Rate 1 creates (as documented in Section III and IV), and which Rate 6 fails to satisfactorily address (as documented in Sections V through IX).

<br>

**Q.** What would the Company's volumetric rates be under the proposed Rate HP?

**A.** Rate HP would reduce distribution and transmission rates during the winter months only. Summer rates remain at proposed Rate 1 levels. The following table compares the Company's proposed Rate 1 rates with my proposed Rate HP rates.

|                                                                             | Proposed Rate 1 (¢/kWh) | Rate HP Summer (¢/kWh) | Rate HP Winter (¢/kWh) | Change |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------: | :--------------------: | :--------------------: | :----: |
| **Distribution** — Energy Charge (¢/kWh)                                    | `{python} f"{FILED_DIST_EC*100:.3f}"` | `{python} f"{FILED_DIST_EC*100:.3f}"` | `{python} f"{(r.fair_hp_winter_rate_dist - FILED_RIDERS)*100:.3f}"` | `{python} pct((r.fair_hp_winter_rate_dist - FILED_RIDERS) / FILED_DIST_EC - 1)` |
| **Transmission** — Transmission Service Rate (¢/kWh)                        | `{python} f"{FILED_TX*100:.3f}"` | `{python} f"{FILED_TX*100:.3f}"` | `{python} f"{r.fair_hp_winter_rate_tx*100:.3f}"` | `{python} pct(r.fair_hp_winter_rate_tx / FILED_TX - 1)` |
| **Total delivery volumetric** (distribution + transmission + riders, ¢/kWh) | `{python} f"{FILED_TOTAL_DEL*100:.3f}"` | `{python} f"{FILED_TOTAL_DEL*100:.3f}"` | `{python} f"{(r.fair_hp_winter_rate_dist + r.fair_hp_winter_rate_tx)*100:.3f}"` | `{python} pct((r.fair_hp_winter_rate_dist + r.fair_hp_winter_rate_tx) / FILED_TOTAL_DEL - 1)` |
| **Generation** — Generation Service Charge (¢/kWh)                          | `{python} f"{r.fair_hp_avg_rate_gen*100:.3f}"` | `{python} f"{r.fair_hp_avg_rate_gen*100:.3f}"` | `{python} f"{r.fair_hp_avg_rate_gen*100:.3f}"` | — |

: Rate HP winter rates compared to Rate 1 {#tbl-rate-hp-winter}

Generation rates, the monthly customer charge, and all distribution riders remain the same as under Rate 1, as would summer distribution and transmission rates in the summer.[^riders]

[^riders]: Beyond the distribution energy charge and transmission, Rate 1's volumetric delivery rate carries several pass-through riders: the Competitive Transition Assessment (CTA) and the Public Benefits charges — Systems Benefits Charge (SBC), Conservation Adjustment Mechanism (CAM), Renewable Energy, and the non-bypassable FMCC Delivery Charge. Each adjusts through its own reconciliation clause rather than this rate case; at their filed values (Exhibit CLP-RATES-3, Docket No. 26-05-10) they total `{python} f"{FILED_RIDERS*100:.3f}"` ¢/kWh, and I hold them unchanged under Rate HP. The total delivery rate shown in the table includes these riders. Generation reflects Eversource's standard-service supply rates over the rate case's test year (calendar year 2025). Because those rates vary seasonally, the single figure shown is the kWh-weighted average across the average post-heat-pump load profile, and it is identical under Rate 1 and Rate HP.

<br>

**Q.** Why are the rate reductions concentrated in winter?

**A.** Because the incremental electricity consumption from heat pumps is concentrated in winter. Heat pumps replace fossil-fuel furnaces and boilers, which run primarily during the heating season. In summer, heat pumps provide air conditioning — a service most homes already have to some extent — so summer electricity consumption changes little after installation.

By concentrating the rate reduction in the months when incremental HP load occurs, Rate HP avoids giving a discount to base load. This is more precisely targeted than a year-round flat reduction, but it means the total annual revenue reduction needed to eliminate the overcharge is achieved with a deeper winter rate reduction rather than a shallow year-round rate reduction.

<br>

**Q.** How did you determine the winter rate reductions for each component?

**A.** For each component — distribution and transmission — I asked: what reduction in the winter volumetric rate would make the annual overpayment of the _average_ fossil-fuel-heated customer who installs a heat pump equal to zero? In other words, I found the single winter ¢/kWh rate that, applied to a sample of post-heat-pump load profiles, produces a population-average T&D bill equal to the customer's pre-heat-pump T&D bill plus the incremental marginal T&D cost of serving the new electrified heating load.

Because this is a single rate applied to all customers, it zeroes out overpayment _on average_ — individual customers with different load shapes will still have residual over- or underpayments. I address this issue below.

<br>

**Q.** A `{python} pct(abs((r.fair_hp_winter_rate_dist - FILED_RIDERS) / FILED_DIST_EC - 1))` winter reduction seems large. Why does the winter rate have to fall so steeply in order to eliminate the overpayment?

**A.** When one of the Company's fossil-heated customers installs a heat pump, they cause only `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_dist_delta + r.all_fossil_annual_mc_tx_delta)` in incremental marginal T&D cost per year,[^cr_calc_s3] on average, even though their winter consumption roughly quadruples, which causes their winter T&D bill to roughly quadruple as well. To satisfy cost-causation, the customer's post-heat-pump winter T&D bill should approximately equal their pre-heat-pump-winter T&D bill, plus `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_dist_delta + r.all_fossil_annual_mc_tx_delta)`. To achieve this, the winter rate has to drop by roughly the same factor that winter load goes up. Four times the kWh at a only slightly higher total bill means roughly one-quarter the rate per kWh — a ~75% reduction.

[^cr_calc_s3]: A shown in Section III, @fig-seasonal-mc-all-fossil-comparison.

<br>

**Q.** You said Rate HP makes the _average_ overpayment zero, but does not guarantee that every individual customer's overpayment is zero. How close does it get?

**A.** As close as possible without per-customer block rates.

Under a perfectly fair rate, each customer's post-installation delivery bill would equal their base-load bill plus only the incremental marginal T&D costs their heat pump actually causes — eliminating every individual overpayment entirely. That would require implementing per-customer thresholds, and charging incremental loads at marginal cost.

Rate HP uses a single winter rate for all customers, which is simple, practical, and performs better than the Company's one-size-fits-all block rate — though it does mean some customers will still overpay, and others will underpay, even if the two wash out on average.

@fig-testimony-annual-all-fossil-r1-vs-r6-vs-r6mc-vs-seasonal shows the overpayment distribution across four scenarios. Under Rate 1 (top panel), virtually every heat pump customer overpays. Under Rate 6 as proposed (second panel), the distribution remains wide, shifts modestly leftward, but the average overpayment remains `{python} dollar(op.overpay_mean_rate_6_all_fossil)` per year. Under the modified Rate 6 with Block 2 rates set at marginal cost (third panel), the shift is larger — mean overpayment falls to `{python} dollar(op.overpay_mean_r6_mfc0_trans_all_fossil)`, but delivered fuel and higher-income customers end up underpaying. Under Rate HP (bottom panel), the distribution is centered on zero: the mean overpayment is `{python} dollar(op.overpay_mean_fair_seasonal_all_fossil)`.

:::{.column-page-inset-right}
{{< embed notebooks/overpayment.qmd#fig-testimony-annual-all-fossil-r1-vs-r6-vs-r6mc-vs-seasonal >}}
:::

Individual customers still have residual over- or underpayments — an inherent limitation of any single-rate schedule. However, `{python} pct(op.pct_within_200_seasonal)` of fossil-fuel customers are within $200 of zero.

And unlike either Rate 6, nearly all of the systematic bias is removed: natural-gas customers are almost as likely to be underpaying as overpaying (`{python} pct(op.pct_overpaying_seasonal_natgas)` overpay, vs. `{python} pct(op.pct_overpaying_seasonal_delivered_fuels)` of oil/propane customers), and LMI customers see a similar balance (`{python} pct(op.pct_overpaying_seasonal_lmi)` overpay, vs. `{python} pct(op.pct_overpaying_seasonal_non_lmi)` of non-LMI customers).

In short, Rate HP does what a practical rate design can do: unlike even the version of Rate 6 with discounts set to marginal cost, Rate HP eliminates the overcharge that Rate 1 imposes on heat pump customers _on average_, while leaving a over/underpayment spread that is modest and that doesn't systematically disadvantage natural-gas-heated and low income customers.

<br>


## XI. Impact of Rate HP on Heat Pump Operating Costs

<br>

**Q.** Under the proposed Rate HP, what would happen to the average natural-gas-heated household’s total annual energy bills when they switch to a heat pump, compared with Rate 1?

## XII. Enrollment: How Customers Get onto Rate HP

<br>

**Q.** How would customers be enrolled in the proposed Rate HP?

**A.** I recommend two enrollment channels, both automatic.

**Every new customer that installs a heat pump** should be auto-enrolled in Rate HP at the time of installation. To achieve this, every customer receiving a heat pump incentive through Energize CT or the New England Heat Pump Accelerator should be placed on Rate HP automatically. For installations that happen outside of Energize CT — for example, self-funded purchases — the Company should provide an attestation and certification pathway: a simple form the installer or customer submits to confirm a qualifying heat pump was installed.

**For existing heat pump customers**, the Company should auto-enroll all known electric customers who have previously installed heat pumps. These customers are being overcharged right now. Since the day they installed their heat pump, they have been paying far more than the T&D costs caused by their new load. And a portion of these customers are readily identifiable by the Company, those that previously received a heat pump incentive through EnergizeCT or any other relevant state or utility program. There is no reason to delay correcting this.

After a customer is auto-enrolled, Rate HP would be opt-out: the customer could return to Rate 1 (or any other optional rate) if they choose.

<br>

**Q.** Why do you recommend automatic enrollment rather than an opt-in rate?

**A.** Because opt-in rates fail. They require customers to know the rate exists, understand that it would save them money, and take affirmative action to enroll. Most customers never do.

This is not a theoretical concern. Maine's Central Maine Power offered a seasonal heat pump rate on an opt-in basis. Enrollment never exceeded 2% of eligible customers.[^cmp_pilot]

[^cmp_pilot]: Shah, Wagner & Teener, "Designing Better Rates for Heat Pump Customers,"
RMI (June 17, 2026) [@Designing_better_rates_shah_2026]. CMP's seasonal heat pump rate launched January 2023 with a 5,000-
customer enrollment cap. Maine had approximately 143,000 heat pumps installed statewide
by the end of 2024. Even with active marketing, only about 2,100 enrolled.

New York's experience is even more striking. Con Edison has facilitated more than 43,000 heat pump installations through its Clean Heat program, yet as of December 2025, only about 500 households — barely 1% — had enrolled in the utility's opt-in Steady Use Rate, which is designed to save a typical heat pump customer roughly $500 per year.[^coned_steady_use] That is $131 million in cumulative bill savings left on the table over the rate period, simply because customers did not know the rate existed or found the enrollment process confusing.

[^coned_steady_use]: Environmental Defense Fund, Rewiring America & Alliance for a Green Economy, "Con Edison Heat Pump Customers Missing Out on $131 Million in Bill Savings" (July 9, 2025) [@edfrewiringagree_ConEdisonHeat_2025]. Enrollment figure of ~500 as of December 2025 reported in Mona Zhang, "How NY heat pump users got stuck with higher bills," E&E News (March 3, 2026) [@HowNYHeatPumpUsersGotStuckWithHigherBills_Zhang_2026].

The goal of offering heat pump rates by creating Rate HP is to eliminate the existing cross-subsidy between heat pump customers and fossil-heating customers, and to prevent customers newly installing heat pumps from overpaying in the first place. **But creating a new rate schedule does not automatically solve the problem — the rate needs to be adopted at scale. And if a heat pump rate isn't paired with auto-enrollment, it won't be.**

Massachusetts avoided the opt-in trap entirely by building auto-enrollment into its heat pump rate from the start. In DPU 25-08, the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities approved a lower heat pump rate for the state's three investor-owned electric utilities — Eversource, Unitil, and National Grid.[^ma_hp_rate] Customers who install heat pumps through Mass Save — the state's ratepayer-funded efficiency program — are automatically enrolled at the time of installation. For customers who installed heat pumps before the program existed, Massachusetts uses an attestation process.

[^ma_hp_rate]: The Massachusetts DPU maintains an overview of the seasonal heat pump rates and enrollment procedures for all three IOUs at @dpu_ResidentialElectricSeasonal_2025.

We know that opt-in rates get low enrollment; the Company can and must design a better enrollment mechanism: automatic enrollment through Energize CT and the New England Heat Pump Accelerator. Every heat pump customer who is _not_ enrolled continues to be overcharged by the full amount every year.

<br>

**Q.** Could automatic enrollment cause some heat pump customers to see higher bills?

**A.** No, because Rate HP is specifically designed so that _every heat pump customer pays less than they would under Rate 1_. By lowering Rate 1's existing winter rates, no heat pump customer would be made worse off by being placed on Rate HP.

This is the key link between rate design and enrollment. A rate that only _lowers_ charges can be safely applied to all heat pump customers without risk of adverse bill impacts. If the rate raised some charges and lowered others — for example, a higher fixed charge paired with a lower volumetric rate — some customers could see higher bills in certain months. The seasonal winter reduction avoids this entirely: summer rates are unchanged, and winter rates are only lower. There are no structural losers.

A rate design that only lowers charges unlocks auto-enrollment, but it necessarily constrains eligibility: it must be a tech-specific rate, rather than one available to all residential customers. A lower rate is justified for heat pump customers. As covered in section III, they are structural "high-usage" customers who would otherwise overpay. A lower rate available to all customers would simply lower the bills of anyone who enrolled, which would create a revenue shortfall under heavy enrollment.

I believe this is the right trade-off. A rate that can be safely auto-enrolled to every eligible customer, even if restricted to a defined population, will reach far more people and thus have a fundamentally bigger impact than an optional rate with a revenue-neutral design (like a high fixed charge) that is available to all customers but which will achieve negligible enrollment, because it requires customers to discover it, evaluate it, and opt in.

<br>

**Q.** Why is it important to auto-enroll existing heat pump customers, not just new ones?

**A.** Because enrolling only new customers stops the cross-subsidy from getting bigger, but it does not fix it for the customers who are already bearing it.

If the Commission only enrolls new heat pump customers going forward, every customer who has _already_ installed a heat pump continues to be overcharged by the full amount, indefinitely — unless they opt in on their own, which as I have discussed, many of them will not. The per-household stakes are substantial: `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge)` per year in combined T&D overcharges. These are real dollars being transferred from heat pump customers to fossil-heating customers every year, and they have been accumulating since the day each customer installed their heat pump.

The Company and Energize CT have records of past heat pump incentive recipients. For customers who installed heat pumps outside of incentive programs, an attestation process — as Massachusetts uses — can identify them. Auto-enrollment of existing heat pump customers is what makes this proposal a genuine fix rather than a half-measure.


## XIII. Discussion of Alternative Rate Designs

<br>

**Q.** The heat pump rate you propose in Rate HP is a seasonal design, lowering winter transmission and distribution rates. Are there other rate designs that can eliminate the cross-subsidy?

**A.** Yes, and I considered several before arriving at this recommendation. But any viable solution must solve two problems simultaneously: the **overpayment problem** — by stopping the overcollection of transmission and distribution revenue from heat pump customers — and the **enrollment problem** — ensure that the customers who are actually being overcharged are actually on the rate that fixes it. These two constraints significantly narrow the design space.

There are two broad categories of solutions: **default rate redesign**, which changes Rate 1 for all residential customers, and **tech-specific rates**, which create a new schedule for heat pump customers only. Each approach has different strengths and weaknesses on the overpayment and enrollment dimensions. I will discuss each in turn.

<br>

**Q.** Could the cross-subsidy be eliminated by redesigning Rate 1?

**A.** The main virtue of the default rate redesign approach is that it solves the enrollment problem directly: if you managed to eliminate the overpayment by redesigning Rate 1, the vast majority of residential customers are already on this rate, so you would fix the problem at scale without requiring anyone to change anything.

The difficulty is that the main lever for reducing the overpayment within Rate 1 is raising the fixed charge. Raising the customer charge shifts revenue recovery away from volumetric rates, which reduces the per-kWh overcollection on high-usage customers.

The problem is magnitude. To eliminate the heat pump overpayment by redesigning Rate 1, the monthly fixed charge would then have to rise from `{python} dollar(fc.original_fixed_charge, accuracy=2)` to `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge, accuracy=2)` — an increase of `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge_delta, accuracy=2)` per month.

This is a massive change that would affect every residential customer, not just heat pump customers, and would be regressive to low-income households unless paired with an income-graduated structure.

To put that in perspective, the Company's own MCOS supports a marginal customer cost of $28.98 per month for Rate 1.[^nieto-mcos-cc] Yet for Rate 1, the Company proposes moving the customer charge from $9.62 to just $12.36 — a $2.74 step toward a $16.62 gap.[^davis-parsons-mrcc] At that pace, the fixed charge would not approach the level needed to eliminate the heat pump cross-subsidy (`{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge, accuracy=2)`) for many decades to come.

[^nieto-mcos-cc]: Exhibit CLP-MCOS-1 [@eversource_Docket260510Exhibit_2026], Table 1: Rate 1 marginal customer cost = `$28.98`/month.

[^davis-parsons-mrcc]: Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons, Exhibit CLP-RATES-1 [@_Docket260510Exhibit_c], Section IV.B. Current Rate 1 customer charge of `$9.62` proposed to increase to `$12.36` per the MRCC calculation in Exhibit CLP-RATES-2.13.

<br>

**Q.** What about the tech-specific approach? What design levers does it offer, and why?

**A.** Within the default rate, where revenue sufficiency must be maintained, the only way to reduce overcollection from heat pump customers is to raise the fixed charge on everyone, shifting revenue recovery away from per-kWh rates.

And the Company could choose to create a tech-specific rate exclusively for heat pump customers with a high fixed-charge design. Indeed, Rate 6 takes a step in this direction, by raising the fixed charge from $12.36 to $30.95.

But a tech-specific rate opens an additional lever for reducing overcollection that the default rate (or any rate that must be revenue neutral with respect to the residential class as a whole) does not have: keep the fixed charge the same, and simply lower volumetric charges.

If the overcollection problem arises from the application of volumetric rates _designed for the average electric customer_ to a subclass of residential customers with structurally _above-average_ usage, then simply lowering the volumetric rates for that population reduces overcollection from that population. Put another way, instead of fundamentally changing the rate design for Rate 1, you can simply recalibrate it, by designing the volumetric rate component for the average heat pump customer, rather than the average residential customer.

<br>

**Q.** How do each of these two kinds of tech-specific rates — raising the fixed charge vs. just lowering the volumetric rates — affect the enrollment problem?

**A.** Unlike redesigning Rate 1, a tech-specific rate does not solve enrollment automatically — customers must enroll onto it. And as I showed in Section XII, auto-enrollment is the only realistic solution to reaching meaningful participation with an optional rate.

I am working under the assumption that the Commission is more likely to approve auto-enrollment if the rate design guarantees that no enrolled customer is made worse off.

A version of Rate HP with a very high fixed charge could cause a minority of heat pump customers — particularly lower-usage ones — to see higher bills in certain months. Lower volumetric rates guarantee the opposite: every enrolled customer either saves or pays the same in a given month, depending on the design, but no customer pays more in any month.

In other words, tech-specific heat pump rates with lower volumetric charges would allow the Commission to achieve the benefits of auto-enrollment without paying the cost of creating structural losers.

<br>

**Q.** Are there different ways to structure the lower volumetric charges under a tech-specific rate?

**A.** Yes. There are three main designs, each of which can eliminate the overpayment, if volumetric rates are lowered to the right level:

1. **Flat** — lower all non-generation volumetric rates by whatever percentage is needed to eliminate the annual overpayment. The rates would still be flat, so they would be the same for every hour of the year. This is the simplest option.
2. **Seasonal** — leave the summer rate unchanged and lower only the winter rate. **This is what I propose.** This is also how Massachusetts has designed their heat pump rates.
3. **Time-of-use** — create a heat-pump-specific version of a TOU rate that would have lower on-peak and off-peak rates compared with a TOU rate designed to be revenue-neutral for the residential class as a whole (such as Rate 7), layering TOU price signals onto the tech-specific reduction.

All three solve the overpayment problem as long as the resulting per-kWh rates are set low enough to stop overcollecting from the average heat pump customer.

I'll discuss the costs and benefits of each design in turn.

<br>

**Q.** Given these options, why do you not propose a flat tech-specific rate?

**A.** A tech-specific rate with a flat volumetric charge that is lower year-round, paired with auto-enrollment, solves both the overpayment and enrollment problems, and it does so with the simplest available design. It eliminates the overcharge, guarantees savings for every enrolled customer, and is simple enough that customers, the Commission, and the Company can all verify that it works. While this would remove the annual overpayment paid by heat pump customers on average, it would do so by reducing the T&D bills of heat pump customers by a uniform percentage in every month, including those in summer. I share the Company's objective of pricing incremental heat pump loads at (closer to) marginal cost, in order to satisfy cost-causation principles. Doing this would "right-size" post-heat-pump T&D bills during the heating season, since that is where `{python} pct(r.all_fossil_pct_incremental_kwh_oct_apr)` of incremental heat pump load occurs for the average customer switching from fossil fuels (October through April).

<br>

**Q.** Why do you advocate for a seasonal tech-specific rate?

**A.** In addition to the benefits of a flat tech-specific rate — solving the overpayment and enrollment problems — a seasonal rate has two main benefits:

1. Seasonal rates are targeted: as we saw in Section III, most of the overcollection occurs during winter. Lowering rates in winter reduces overcollection from the season where most of it occurs, rather than year round.
2. Seasonal rates promote bill stability: winter is when new heat pump customers see their electric bills rise most sharply — the heat pump replaces a gas furnace, so electricity consumption increases significantly during heating months. A seasonal rate concentrates the bill relief in exactly those months, smoothing out the seasonal bill shock that might otherwise discourage adoption or cause customers to question whether the heat pump was a good investment (even if they are saving money by switching overall).

**Q.** How could the Company design a seasonal tech-specific heat pump rate correctly?

**A.** Designing a seasonal heat pump rate correctly requires satisfying three conditions:

1. The seasonal rate must _lower_ what heat pump customers pay annually. Some seasonal designs try to maintain revenue-neutrality for heat pump customers by lowering the winter rate but raising the summer rate, which merely shifts the overpayment between seasons, defeating the entire purpose of a heat pump rate.
2. The seasonal rate must lower what heat pump customers pay annually _by a sufficient amount to eliminate the overpayment_. Reducing the winter rate by 1 c/kWh, for example, would be a half-measure.
3. While rates in both seasons can be lowered — the reduced revenue collection doesn't all have to concentrate in winter — neither season's rates should be set higher than those in Rate 1, as that could produce structural losers, thus complicating auto-enrollment — even if the rate satisfies the first two conditions.


<br>

**Q.** Why do you not recommend the other approaches you discussed?

**A.** Each of the alternatives I have discussed in this section could eliminate the overpayment problem in theory. In practice, they either complicate auto-enrollment, or require significant disruption to all residential customers in order to make a difference. In other words: given the downsides of these alternatives, they would likely leave the cross-subsidy largely intact.

A **redesigned Rate 1** would require raising the fixed charge by an amount I do not believe the Commission is prepared to approve in this case, particularly without introducing income-graduation to avoid regressive impacts. If the Commission took this approach, the most likely outcome would be a marginal increase in the fixed charge that would look like progress but do essentially nothing to remove the overpayment and fix heat pump operating costs.

A **tech-specific rate with a high fixed charge** could strike customers as unfamiliar and would create structural losers among lower-usage heat pump customers, complicating auto-enrollment. And without auto-enrollment, creating an optional heat pump rate (that almost no customers opt into) risks allowing stakeholders to claim victory without having any meaningful impact on the problem.

A **tech-specific TOU rate** does not solve the overcollection problem on its own; it would need significantly lower volumetric rates than a TOU rate design for the residential class as a whole (such as Rate 7) to actually eliminate the overcharge. (The reason is simple: the overpayment problem arises from an overreliance on volumetric rates applied to structurally high-usage customers. Making a volumetric rate time-varying does not change this — it still has to be significantly lowered.) While a properly designed TOU rate for heat pump customers would create incentives for load shifting as well as removing the overpayment, it would also add complexity and may create structural losers, unlike a seasonal tech-specific rate. Unless the Commission is prepared to create a properly designed tech-specific TOU rate with rates low enough to eliminate the overcharge, auto-enroll all heat pump customers onto it, and do so in a timely fashion, this route risks allowing the perfect to become the enemy of the good.

<br>
